Show HN: Instance – A clean-room reimplementation of GameMaker 8.1 in Rust
items.summary: I used GameMaker 8.1 a ton in late elementary and middle school, and GML was the first programming language I wrote. I still think it's a fun engine to use because it has so many batteries included. So I built an open-source reimplementation of it in Rust which I'm calling Instance. It opens existing .gmk and .gm81 projects and runs them on Windows, macOS and in the browser, with a more efficient GML interpreter than the original GameMaker. You can try the IDE here in your browser: https://groverburger.github.io/instance/ . It comes with three example games, including Spelunky Classic built from Derek Yu's released source shared under its permissive license. Just change something and press Run to see your edits in action. Old GM games depend on a lot of quirks such as the order events run in, the exact random number generator, how sound_isplaying lags behind the audio. I wrote up the behavior as specs from the documentation, the file formats and black-box tests against the real program, then implemented it from those specs. No proprietary code was disassembled or decompiled. CLEANROOM.md describes the process. It covers most of almost all of 8.1. All the resource editors, GML and drag-and-drop actions, d3d, particles, surfaces, MIDI, mplay multiplayer and DLL calls. It can also export a game as a standalone executable or a single HTML file. Projects can be saved as folders of plain text and PNG files for git. I wrote most of the code with Claude Opus 5.5 over about three weeks. Claude banged out a pretty good reimplementation in a morning, but as always the last 20% took 80% of the work. GameMaker also turns out to work surprisingly well with LLMs. GML is small and simple, and a whole game fits in one project file. I'm happy to answer any questions! Code: https://github.com/groverburger/instance

items.title: Show HN: SlopIt – A blog your coding agent runs
items.summary: Hi HN! This is something I built out of my own need. I’m doing several projects on the side, and many of them need a CMS quickly (automated by my agents), and I thought there’s space for a very minimal thing that’s more agent-native instead of setting up the heavy blogging platforms. A few things that stand out here - you, as a human, cannot post or update your content. You need to tell your agent to do it. It's designed like this on purpose because that's where the industry is going. Although it's named SlopIt a bit tongue-in-cheek, obviously not trying to encourage actual slop here - I think if done the right way, LLM-assisted writing could be as good as human writing (and will only get better over time). Some of the example blogs I've setup for my projects: - https://blog.rafikigo.com/why-we-started-rafikigo/ (Blog for a Kenyan tour company) - https://blog.simbastack.com/ (Blog for my consulting firm) I'd love for you guys to try it out and provide feedback. -- Getting started is super simple - just copy the prompt (shown in the Hero) and drop it into your agent and you have a new blog ready. I do recommend spending some time and effort in using Skills and projects like Humanizer ( https://github.com/blader/humanizer ) to make your content more readable for humans. Oh and the core is open source (MIT) - https://github.com/Simbastack-hq/SlopIt

Show HN: Foldocs, turn a shared Google Drive or Nextcloud folder into a website
items.summary: I built something for someone who needed a website, but didn't want to be exposed to yet another complicated CMS like WordPress. They already use Google Docs, so I built Foldocs for them to publish and maintain a simple website. Foldocs creates static HTML pages out of a (shared) fol der of doc uments in Google Drive (or Nextcloud!): (sub)folders become (sub)sections on the site, and documents inside them become pages. Does it work? Proof is to be found in the pudding: Foldocs.com, the site that explains Foldocs, is itself a Foldocs site! The underlying Google Drive is here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ZRYhiIGfSeIcA_gjRVgT... . Foldocs is an open source (AGPL 3.0) Python engine anyone can run. It currently supports three themes, dark mode, and an RSS feed. You can also try it out by creating a preview on https://try.foldocs.com . Paste a shared folder link, and see a preview (kept for 7 days, limited in files / size, and only syncs manually). Previews are running on a separate domain and a throwaway VPS, since hosting strangers' content on the internet is... scary. Curious to hear what you think of the concept, learn what breaks (but don't try too hard please), what you run into, and/or what is missing!
